summary:
Mission Designer is an interactive web game that lets players design a complete space mission end to end: choosing a scientific objective, selecting an orbit and launch vehicle, building a spacecraft, equipping instruments and communications, and then running a simulation that produces a full mission report. It supports solo play or team play with up to four role based players who must negotiate trade offs together in real time.

Under the hood, a shared rules engine computes mass, energy, battery life, data return, cost, and schedule, flagging design problems with plain language explanations of why they matter. This turns abstract systems engineering trade offs into tangible, immediate feedback. For Moon and Mars missions, successful landers unlock a third person rover exploration mode built on real elevation datasets provided through the challenge's resources, including USGS HiRISE data for Mars' Jezero Crater and NASA LOLA data for the lunar south pole, so the rover's performance is driven by the exact components the player designed.

By gamifying the engineering trade offs real mission designers face, such as power versus mass versus science return versus budget, the project makes space mission design intuitive, collaborative, and genuinely educational for students and space enthusiasts alike.
details:
How it works: Mission Designer walks players through the real workflow of planning a space mission. They pick a scientific objective (such as finding water ice on the Moon or searching for signs of past life on Mars), then choose an orbit and launch vehicle, assemble a spacecraft from real component categories (power, propulsion, communications, instruments), and run a month by month simulation with reproducible random events. The engine calculates mass, energy balance, battery autonomy, data return, cost, and schedule, and explains in plain language why each design choice helps or hurts the mission. If a lander successfully touches down on the Moon or Mars, the report unlocks a third person rover exploration mode where the player drives across real terrain, built from NASA and USGS elevation datasets of Jezero Crater and the lunar south pole, using exactly the components they designed: battery life limits range, solar panels or an RTG determine recharging, and the radio determines how much science data makes it back to Earth.

Benefits and impact: The game turns dense aerospace engineering concepts, power versus mass versus cost versus science return, into something anyone can learn by doing, making it a tool for STEM outreach, classrooms, and science museums. Because players negotiate trade offs live in team mode, it also teaches collaboration and communication skills that mirror how real mission teams operate at NASA and partner agencies.

Tools and technology: The project is a single full stack JavaScript application built with React and react-three-fiber (Three.js) for the 3D visualization, Express and Socket.io for the multiplayer server and real time room synchronization, and Vite for the build pipeline. A shared rules engine (plain JavaScript, no framework) runs identically in the browser for solo play and on the server for team play, so the server always has the authoritative state. Elevation data was processed from NASA's LOLA lunar dataset and USGS's HiRISE Mars DTM mosaic using custom Node.js scripts that fetch only the needed byte ranges and convert them into lightweight heightmaps.

Creativity: Rather than presenting mission design as a spreadsheet of numbers, the project frames it as a cooperative, role based game where no single player controls every system, forcing genuine negotiation. The payoff for a good design is not just a score but a playable rover sequence on scientifically accurate terrain, so the consequences of engineering decisions become something the player can literally drive through.

Factors considered: The team prioritized scientific accuracy (using real elevation datasets and plausible mission parameters derived from public data), accessibility (support for five languages: Spanish, English, German, French, and Italian), and replayability (seeded random events and multiple mission targets). The architecture was also designed so that once official challenge datasets become available, they can replace the current placeholder JSON files with minimal code changes.
